title: Why Static Skill Inconsistencies Do Not Equate to Runtime Risks: A Behavioral Analysis of LLM Agent Execution

paper.title: Why Static Skill Inconsistencies Do Not Equate to Runtime Risks: A Behavioral Analysis of LLM Agent Execution
paper.abstract: Abstract. LLM agent frameworks heavily rely on external skill assets to standardize tool usage, encode operational workflows, and supply executable runtime resources. Despite their widespread adoption, multi-component skill packages frequently suffer from cross-artifact inconsistencies, where documentation, scripts, and configuration files specify conflicting behavioral constraints. Although static auditing techniques can uncover such contractual discrepancies, static defect volume cannot reliably reflect real-world agent performance degradation. This gap leaves practitioners without rigorous evidence to assess the practical risk of flawed agent skills. This paper presents a systematic empirical study to demystify the runtime implications of skill inconsistencies. We conduct large-scale auditing over 575 community and benchmark skills, yielding 1,182 manually validated contract inconsistencies. We further build a controlled evaluation pipeline with 49 executable agent tasks and three representative LLMs across NoSkill, OriginalSkill, and FixedSkill experimental settings. Through fine-grained behavioral analysis of 441 paired execution trajectories, we quantify the actual performance impacts of resolved defects. Our empirical results reveal that contractual conflicts are pervasive in practical skill ecosystems, impacting over 64% of all examined skills. Skill repairing consistently improves task success rates, yet the performance benefits exhibit strong model heterogeneity, ranging from substantial improvement to negligible gain. Further trajectory dissection indicates that nearly all execution instances expose inconsistent skill content, which rules out exposure frequency as the source of performance variance. Instead, cross-model behavioral differences after inconsistency exposure dominate final task outcomes. We find that weaker models frequently follow erroneous skill specifications and propagate defects into final results, while stronger models actively mitigate runtime errors. Our findings demonstrate that the practical risk of flawed skills is jointly determined by execution reachability and agent post-execution behavior, rather than static inconsistency quantity alone.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Why Agent Skills Matter. LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable components to acquire procedural knowledge, tool-use capabilities, and domain-specific workflows. Agent Skills are an important artifact in this emerging ecosystem ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2026a ) . Unlike one-off prompts, a Skill is typically distributed as a reusable package containing documentation, metadata, scripts, configuration files, and other resources ( Anthropic, 2026 ; Anthropic, 2025b ) . Together, these artifacts specify how the Skill should be discovered, interpreted, and executed. As the public Skill ecosystem rapidly expands, the same Skill may be reused across different tasks and agents, allowing quality issues to affect multiple downstream executions. This multi-artifact structure also introduces a new reliability challenge. Because individual artifacts can evolve independently, they may make incompatible claims about the same functionality, interface, or runtime requirement. For example, documentation may promise a capability that the implementation does not provide, or different documents may specify conflicting dependency versions. We refer to such cases as Skill contract inconsistencies . Unlike conventional specification-implementation mismatches, these inconsistencies may arise between a Skill and its environment, across documentation artifacts, or between documentation and code. Do Static Inconsistencies Matter at Runtime? Detecting a static inconsistency does not imply that it will cause runtime harm. Static inspection can establish that two artifacts conflict, but it cannot determine whether the conflict will enter actual execution or whether it will ultimately affect task outcomes or execution cost. A static finding therefore indicates a potential problem, not its actual runtime risk. This distinction has direct practical consequences. If all inconsistencies are treated equally, limited auditing and repair effort cannot be prioritized toward findings that actually affect execution, while low-impact findings may obscure more consequential ones. Skill quality assessment therefore needs to move beyond finding detection toward runtime risk prioritization. Existing work has examined Skill structure ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , documentation quality ( Li et al., 2026a ) , security ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026b ) , and artifact-level defects ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Meng et al., 2026 ) . However, there is still limited evidence on whether such static findings enter agent execution, whether repairing them changes runtime outcomes, and how agents respond after exposure. We therefore lack a systematic understanding of how static defects translate into runtime consequences : how prevalent Skill contract inconsistencies are, how much they affect agent execution, and why these effects arise. Our Study and Key Findings. To answer these questions, we conduct an empirical study of Skill contract inconsistencies. First, we collect 575 Skills from GitHub and SkillBench ( Li et al., 2026a ) and develop a taxonomy spanning three contract boundaries: Environment, Inter Document, and Document Code. Through automated auditing and manual validation, we confirm 1,182 inconsistencies and characterize their prevalence, types, and distribution. Second, we construct 49 verifiable tasks from real-world Skills and evaluate three models under three conditions: NoSkill , OriginalSkill , and FixedSkill . The comparison between OriginalSkill and FixedSkill estimates the runtime effect of the targeted inconsistency, while NoSkill separates this effect from the general benefit of using a Skill. Finally, we analyze paired execution trajectories to trace whether inconsistencies enter execution and how different responses relate to final outcomes. Our study yields four main findings. ❶ Skill contract inconsistencies are widespread and unevenly distributed. At least one inconsistency appears in 67.4% of GitHub Skills and 64.4% of SkillBench Skills. In SkillBench, Document Code inconsistencies account for 56.2% of all findings, with over_promised alone accounting for 45.6%. ❷ Fixing inconsistencies improves average task effectiveness for all three models, but the magnitude varies substantially. Claude Haiku 4.5 ( Anthropic, 2025a ) , Qwen3.6-35B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ; oMLX, 2026 ) , and DeepSeek-V4-Flash ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026 ; Continuum Labs, 2026 ; Hanks, 2026 ) improve by 0.136, 0.085, and 0.023 score points, respectively. The runtime impact of an inconsistency is therefore not a fixed property of the Skill alone. ❸ These cross-model differences are not explained by Skill exposure. Across 441 paired executions, agents read the Skill in 97.1% of runs. Exposure rates are similarly high for Haiku, Qwen, and DeepSeek at 98%, 93%, and 100%, respectively. ❹ The models diverge primarily after contact. Haiku, Qwen, and DeepSeek follow the inconsistency into failure in 30%, 24%, and 12% of runs, respectively, while DeepSeek recovers in 56% of exposed runs. The key distinction is therefore not whether an agent encounters the inconsistency, but how it responds after exposure. Taken together, these findings show that static inconsistency count is a poor proxy for runtime risk. Runtime impact depends not only on whether an inconsistency exists, but also on whether it enters execution and how the agent responds after contact. Skill quality assessment should therefore move beyond counting static findings toward distinguishing their actual runtime risks. Contributions. In summary, this work makes the following contributions: ∙ \bullet A taxonomy and large-scale empirical characterization of Skill contract inconsistencies. We develop a taxonomy spanning three artifact boundaries and systematically analyze 1,182 manually confirmed inconsistencies across 575 real-world and benchmark Skills. ∙ \bullet A controlled evaluation of the runtime impact of Skill inconsistencies. We construct 49 real-world tasks and quantify the effects of inconsistencies on task effectiveness and execution efficiency across three models under NoSkill , OriginalSkill , and FixedSkill conditions. ∙ \bullet An execution-level account of how static inconsistencies translate into runtime impact. Through trajectory analysis, we trace inconsistencies from exposure to outcome and show that cross-model differences arise from post-exposure behavior rather than Skill exposure itself.

sections.heading: 2.1. Agent Skills
sections.text: Agent Skills are reusable execution units that provide LLM agents with structured procedural knowledge, tool usage logic, and domain-specific task workflows. Unlike ordinary prompts that provide guidance for a single request, a Skill packages multiple interdependent artifacts into a self-contained unit that an agent can discover, load, and execute. A typical Skill is organized as a directory centered on a SKILL.md file. Its YAML frontmatter specifies metadata such as the Skill name, functionality, applicable scenarios, and dependencies, while the body describes execution steps, constraints, and expected outcomes. A Skill may also include scripts, configuration files, static resources, and other supporting artifacts. Figure 1 . The workflow of using Skills. As shown in Figure 1 , an agent first identifies candidate Skills for a given task and determines their applicability from the associated metadata. It then reads the relevant instructions and resources, executes the prescribed workflow or code, and completes the task according to the requirements stated by the Skill. A Skill is therefore more than a single textual prompt. Its documentation, code, resources, and environment requirements collectively define its expected behavior, while these artifacts may evolve independently. Reliable Skill execution depends not only on the correctness of each artifact, but also on whether they remain consistent about the same behavioral requirements.

sections.heading: 2.2. A Motivating Example
sections.text: From the perspective of an executing agent, the documentation, metadata, code, and resources packaged within a Skill collectively form an implicit Skill contract . This contract specifies the behavioral commitments made by the Skill, including its functionality, inputs and outputs, execution procedure, dependencies, and runtime requirements. A Skill contract combines natural language, semi-structured configuration, and executable code. We define a contract inconsistency as a case in which two or more artifacts make incompatible claims about the same contract property. Such inconsistencies may arise between environment requirements and actual dependencies, across documentation artifacts, or between documentation and code. However, the static presence of an inconsistency does not imply runtime failure. File inspection can establish that conflicting claims exist, but it cannot determine whether the inconsistency will enter the agent’s execution path or what effect it will eventually have. Figure 2 . A real-world Skill. ① marks an Inter Document inconsistency, while ② and ③ mark Document Code inconsistencies. To illustrate this problem, we use the real-world d3-visualization Skill. Figure 2 shows three inconsistencies that can be identified through static inspection. ❶ Document-internal version conflict. One part of the documentation states that the Skill uses D3.js v6, while another specifies d3@7.9.0 as the default dependency. These statements make incompatible claims about the same dependency version and therefore form an Inter Document inconsistency. ❷ Document Code inconsistency in sorting behavior. The documentation requires deterministic sorting before binding input rows to visual elements. However, bubble_chart_example.js directly constructs a Set from the input values without performing the required sorting. The resulting element order may therefore depend on the input order. ❸ Document Code inconsistency in force layout determinism. The documentation requires a fixed number of iterations, deterministic initial positions, and termination after the specified number of iterations. The corresponding code neither fixes the initial randomness nor enforces the specified iteration count. It therefore cannot guarantee the deterministic behavior described by the documentation. This example leads to three observations. Observation 1. Skill contract inconsistencies are not limited to documentation and code. The first inconsistency exists entirely within the documentation and does not involve implementation behavior. This shows that Skill inconsistencies extend beyond conventional specification implementation mismatches. Understanding consistency problems in Skills therefore requires examining conflicts across multiple artifact boundaries. Observation 2. Static detectability does not reveal runtime impact. All three inconsistencies can be detected before execution, yet static evidence cannot determine whether they affect agent execution. It remains unclear whether such inconsistencies reduce task effectiveness, increase execution cost, or affect agents with different capabilities differently. Detecting an inconsistency therefore establishes only that a potential problem exists, not how much it matters at runtime. Observation 3. Final outcomes do not explain how runtime impact arises. Even when an inconsistency is associated with a change in task outcome, success or failure does not explain how that effect arises. We do not know whether the inconsistency enters the agent’s execution path or how the agent responds after encountering the content. Understanding this process requires tracing how the inconsistency propagates through execution and how the agent responds to it. Together, these observations reveal three open questions. We need to understand what inconsistencies exist in real Skills, how much they affect agent execution, and how those effects arise. We therefore ask the following Research Questions (RQs): ∙ \bullet RQ1 (Prevalence and Characteristics). How prevalent are contract inconsistencies in Agent Skills, and what forms do they take? ∙ \bullet RQ2 (Runtime Impact). To what extent do Skill contract inconsistencies affect the task effectiveness and execution efficiency of agents with different capabilities? ∙ \bullet RQ3 (Impact Mechanisms). When and why do Skill contract inconsistencies affect agent execution?

sections.heading: 3. Study Methodology
sections.text: Figure 3 provides an end-to-end overview of our study pipeline. We first build a Skill dataset from GitHub and SkillBench and identify contract inconsistencies through taxonomy-guided SkillAudit and manual validation. RQ1 characterizes the prevalence, types, and distribution of these confirmed findings. We then transform selected real-world inconsistencies into triggerable and verifiable runtime tasks and construct minimally repaired counterparts. RQ2 evaluates their effects on task effectiveness and execution efficiency under NoSkill , OriginalSkill , and FixedSkill conditions. Finally, RQ3 analyzes paired execution trajectories to determine how inconsistencies enter execution and how agents respond after exposure. Figure 3 . The Study pipeline of the paper.

sections.heading: 3.1.1. GitHub Skill Collection.
sections.text: We sample community-maintained Skills from open-source GitHub repositories, prioritizing repositories with high star counts as a proxy for community visibility and practical use. To capture structural differences, we divide candidate Skills into two groups. Document-only Skills contain only Markdown documentation, without executable scripts or supplementary resources. Resource-augmented Skills additionally include internal artifacts such as scripts, configuration files, or other supporting resources. To reduce repository-level bias, we sample at most three Skills from each repository. We inspect Skill metadata and functional descriptions during selection and avoid choosing highly overlapping Skills from the same repository. This process yields 488 GitHub Skills.

sections.heading: 3.1.2. SkillBench Collection.
sections.text: We further include 87 Skills from SkillBench ( Li et al., 2026a ) . Unlike community Skills that evolve naturally on GitHub, SkillBench Skills are manually authored and paired with explicit task objectives and ground-truth specifications, providing a more controlled Skill corpus. This difference provides a useful contrast for RQ1. The GitHub corpus reflects consistency problems that arise during real-world development and maintenance, whereas SkillBench is manually constructed and reviewed, and therefore represents a more controlled artifact-quality setting. Comparing the two allows us to examine whether contract inconsistencies are primarily artifacts of real-world maintenance noise or remain common even in curated Skills.

sections.heading: 3.1.3. Data Summary.
sections.text: Across both sources, we obtain 575 Skills, as shown in Table 1 . Following the taxonomy used by SkillBench ( Li et al., 2026a ) , we categorize them into eight domains: Software Engineering, Media & Content Production, Finance & Economics, Cybersecurity, Office & White Collar Work, Industrial & Physical Systems, Natural Science, and Mathematics & Operations Research.

sections.heading: 3.2. Skill Contract Inconsistency Identification
sections.text: RQ1 first requires a consistent definition of Skill contract inconsistency and a reliable way to identify such cases at scale. We therefore construct an inconsistency taxonomy, operationalize it through a taxonomy-guided static audit pipeline, and manually validate the resulting findings. Figure 4 . Taxonomy of skill - level inconsistencies.

sections.heading: 3.2.1. Taxonomy Of Skill Inconsistency
sections.text: We construct the taxonomy through iterative qualitative analysis ( Raj et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . Starting from real-world Skill artifacts, including documentation, configuration, and source code, we manually inspect misalignment patterns and synthesize them with known issue patterns from tool-agent and API-contract literature ( Kiecker et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . During iteration, we merge redundant categories, eliminate overlapping definitions, and refine the decision criteria for each class. We first classify inconsistencies by the participants of the violated contract: ∙ \bullet Environmental layer: Skill vs. runtime environment. ∙ \bullet Inter-document layer: conflicts among descriptive documents. ∙ \bullet Document-code layer: documentation vs. implementation. Within the Document-code layer, we further classify inconsistencies by the direction of deviation: ∙ \bullet Over-promised (Doc > > Code). The documentation promises functionality, constraints, or behavior that the implementation does not provide. ∙ \bullet Semantically-conflicting (Doc ≠ \neq Code). The documentation and implementation both specify the relevant behavior but contradict each other semantically. ∙ \bullet Under-promised (Doc < < Code). The implementation provides capabilities that are not documented. Because this study focuses on contract violations that may affect agent execution, we primarily retain over-promised and semantically-conflicting cases. Under-promised cases are typically benign ( He et al., 2026 ) and are suppressed by default. We also exclude failures caused purely by agent hallucination or external-service faults ( Tian and Chen, 2026 ) , as these do not originate from inconsistency among Skill artifacts. The resulting taxonomy is shown in Figure 4 .

sections.heading: 3.2.2. Audit Tool
sections.text: To audit skill consistency, we design an tool named SkillAudit. SkillAudit operationalizes the proposed inconsistency taxonomy in 3.2.1 . It takes a skill package as input and outputs ranked findings mapped directly to canonical taxonomy classes. The tool performs purely static analysis without executing the target skill or requiring ground truth. Its pipeline comprises four sequential modules sharing a unified intermediate representation: ❶ Package Comprehension. This module parses documentation and source code into a structured SkillMap. A scanner first validates the target directory (requiring at least one ‘SKILL.md‘), filters out metadata, caches and binaries, and retains partial file contents for indexing. A two-round LLM agent then builds the SkillMap of components, sub-skills and relations: round one selects files for full reading; round two generates the structured map. The SkillMap is cached via content hashing to eliminate redundant model calls for unchanged packages. ❷ Inconsistency Detection. Two groups of checkers identify taxonomy-defined inconsistencies over the same evidence base. Four deterministic checkers perform AST-based code analysis, schema comparison, environment constraint checking, and execution-path URL validation. Five independent LLM checkers target different taxonomy categories and inspect semantic conflicts across artifacts. All detections are normalized to canonical taxonomy labels, while duplicate evidence from different checkers is retained for later aggregation. ❸ Adjudication and Aggregation. This module refines raw detections into structured findings. An adjudicator reviews LLM findings in batches, assigning confirmed or suppressed verdicts with adjusted severity and evidence strength. Rule-based suppression is tracked separately. The adjudicator uses a fail-open design: errors preserve original findings to avoid silent defect loss. Aggregation follows two stages: exact-key deduplication, then semantic clustering by class, location and evidence overlap. Each cluster forms a single root cause entry listing all contributing checkers. ❹ Reporting. The final reporting module produces reports with inconsistencies, root cause statistics, evidence strength distribution, and token usage. Each finding includes a taxonomy label, line-numbered evidence, rationale and evidence strength. Evidence strength is structurally enforced: only verified findings may claim execution blocking. Deterministic checkers run standalone without credentials or network access, ensuring full reproducibility.

sections.heading: 3.2.3. Manual Validation
sections.text: To verify the final auditting results, two authors independently reviewed the audit reports of skills drawn from the full pipeline output of audit tool. with a third resolving disagreements. Of the 575 skills in the datasets, 1182 inconsistencies were confirmed finally.

sections.heading: 3.3. Task Construction
sections.text: WildSkills contains 49 dynamically verifiable task instances, all derived from GitHub Skills. Each task materializes a single re-verified inconsistency so that the experiment focuses on the effect of that inconsistency rather than the overall quality of the Skill. Each task is constructed in five stages. ❶ Selection. Candidate inconsistencies are drawn from manually confirmed GitHub findings. Before inclusion, we re-check the current Skill files to ensure that the target inconsistency still exists and can be localized precisely. ❷ Trigger Design. We write a realistic user request whose most direct solution requires the artifact or code path associated with the target inconsistency. We also size the input so that bypassing the Skill and manually recomputing the result is more expensive than using the Skill, reducing opportunities to sidestep the defect. ❸ Environment. The shipped Skill, project workspace, and input data are packaged into a Docker environment. The Skill is mounted at runtime rather than baked into the image, allowing all experimental conditions to share the same environment while differing only in the provided Skill. ❹ Verifier. Each task includes a deterministic verifier that checks the produced artifact against the target contract using programmatic assertions only. No LLM-as-a-judge is used. ❺ Oracle. We construct a reference solution that passes all verifier checks, confirming that the task itself is solvable and that failure does not arise from an infeasible specification. This process converts a static finding into a repeatable runtime question: what happens when the target inconsistency is placed on a relevant execution path?

sections.heading: 3.3.1. Counterfactual Skill Repair
sections.text: To estimate the runtime impact of each target inconsistency, we construct a minimally repaired FixedSkill for every OriginalSkill . The goal is not to redesign the Skill, but to remove the target inconsistency while changing as little else as possible. The repair strategy depends on the violated contract boundary. For an environmental inconsistency , we align the Skill with the actual runtime environment and pin the relevant requirement. For an inter-document inconsistency , we identify an authoritative statement and unify conflicting descriptions while leaving the implementation unchanged. For a document-code inconsistency , we first determine the intended contract and then modify the implementation to satisfy it. When the documented promise cannot be supported under the target environment, we instead narrow the documentation to match the feasible behavior. All repairs follow two constraints. First, each edit is minimal and confined to the inconsistent element. Second, the repair must not leak the task solution or mirror the verifier. Each WildSkills task therefore has a semantically matched OriginalSkill and FixedSkill , forming the basis for controlled comparison.

sections.heading: 3.4. Models and Experimental Conditions
sections.text: We evaluate three models: DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Their performance on benchmarks and on our NoSkill baseline allows us to examine whether inconsistency impact varies across models, as shown in Table 2 . We emphasize within-model comparisons. The Qwen deployment uses 4-bit quantization, while DeepSeek-V4-Flash runs in its default non-thinking configuration. Absolute cross-model differences should therefore be interpreted with caution. Each task is packaged as a fixed experimental unit containing the user instruction, workspace, Skill directory, deterministic verifier, and oracle solution, and is executed in an isolated Docker container. The agent runs as an unprivileged user, and the Skill directory is injected only at runtime. Table 2 . Models and baseline performance. The paired comparison between OriginalSkill and FixedSkill estimates the runtime effect of the target inconsistency, while NoSkill measures the effect of using the Skill relative to having no Skill. All runs use the same execution harness and a uniform budget covering generation requests, cumulative tokens, and output tokens. Each task-condition combination is executed with three replicates to reduce stochastic variation.

sections.heading: 3.5. Metrics
sections.text: Effectiveness. Our primary metric is verifier pass rate, defined as the fraction of deterministic checks satisfied by the produced artifact, ranging from 0 to 1. For each task-condition pair, we first average the three technical replicates and then perform task-level paired comparisons. The fix effect is defined as Δ = Fixed − Original \Delta=\textsc{Fixed}-\textsc{Original} . This yields 49 paired task-level observations per model. Efficiency. We record cumulative input and output tokens, API calls, agent turns, and wall-clock time. Runs that reach the per-run budget limit are treated as truncated and reported separately. For non-truncated runs, we report median execution costs and additionally use tokens per score point to capture the relationship between computational cost and task effectiveness.

sections.heading: 3.6. Execution Trajectory Collection and Coding
sections.text: We analyse the 441 paired trials used by RQ2 (49 tasks × \times 3 models × \times trials r1–r3), each contrasting OriginalSkill against FixedSkill on an identical task, resolved under the same cell-selection rule as RQ2 (current task-package image, latest study among duplicates). Table 3 . Trajectory coding scheme. Code Definition Exposed Agent reads the skill, either from skills/ or through the Skill tool. Unused Agent never reads the skill and the inconsistency lies outside execution. Bypass Agent is exposed but does not use the inconsistent element. No changed file is executed and no shipped-only form is authored. Follow The inconsistent behaviour reaches the artifact. A tied verifier check fails in OriginalSkill and passes in FixedSkill . Recover The inconsistent behaviour is triggered, but the tied checks still pass. BothFail The tied check fails in both trials and the fix is not decisive. (a) GitHub vs. SkillBench (b) Documentation-only vs. with artifacts Figure 5 . Distribution of confirmed contract inconsistency counts per skill. The y-axis shows the proportion of skills in each bin of per-skill counts. For each task, the fix diff yields three signal types: the files the fix changed, code-like tokens present only in the shipped skill ( shipped-only anchors ), and tokens present only in the fixed skill ( fixed-only anchors ), together with the verifier checks tied to the changed behaviour. A deterministic coder walks each trajectory, separating what the agent authored in tool arguments from what tools returned in file contents or command output, and records skill contact, execution of a changed file, manifestation of shipped-only anchors, per-check verifier failures, and turn-level timestamps. Two decisions carry the analysis throughout. First, contact is not use : reading a file that contains an anchor is not adopting it; only an authored shipped-only form, or execution of a changed file, counts as use. Second, response is attributed by pairing : a behaviour is attributed to the inconsistency only when the FixedSkill arm of the same cell does not exhibit it, which separates the inconsistency’s contribution from a model’s unconditional habits. sections.heading: 4.3. Distribution across skill domains

The size of the gain varies by model. Claude Haiku 4.5 improves the most, rising from 0.741 to 0.877. Qwen3.6-35B improves moderately, from 0.707 to 0.792. DeepSeek-Flash gains the least, from 0.870 to 0.893. Table 7 . Effectiveness across skill conditions on GitHub tasks. Δ \Delta is Fixed minus Original. The task-level breakdown shows that each average gain is driven by a subset of tasks. For Haiku, 30 of 49 tasks improve, 10 stay unchanged, and 9 regress, and the other two models follow the same pattern with fewer improving tasks. For DeepSeek, the small overall delta is not an artifact of aggregation, since the shipped and fixed skills yield identical scores on 30 of 49 tasks. A cross-model comparison adds two observations. The baseline benefit of having any skill is comparable across models, at between + 0.18 +0.18 and + 0.21 +0.21 for all three. The highest-capability model is largely robust, the mid-capability model gains the most, and the lowest-capability model is bounded by its own ceiling. The effect of an inconsistency is therefore a joint property of the contract and the executing model. Finding 5. Task-level effects are highly heterogeneous. The aggregate gains are concentrated on a minority of tasks, so mean deltas understate the cost of inconsistency on the tasks where it actually matters. Per-task analysis is needed to avoid masking this variation.

sections.heading: 5.2. Efficiency
sections.text: Table 8 summarizes efficiency. Fixing the inconsistency does not uniformly reduce runtime cost. For Haiku and Qwen, the fixed condition consumes slightly fewer median tokens and less wall-clock time than the original condition. For DeepSeek-Flash the trend reverses. Fixing the inconsistency raises its median token consumption by 55k and its wall-clock time by 20 seconds, and at 316k tokens and 69 seconds the shipped skill is its cheapest condition. Cost per unit of effectiveness tells a more consistent story. The tokens spent per score point fall from 1.22M to 0.69M for Haiku, from 0.96M to 0.63M for Qwen, and from 0.76M to 0.57M for DeepSeek across the three conditions. For DeepSeek, however, the shipped skill remains its most efficient single condition. Table 8 . Efficiency across skill conditions on GitHub tasks. Model Condition Tokens (med.) The model gradient holds within every type and is steepest in over_promised , where the follow share ranges from 22% for DeepSeek to 50% for Haiku. Of the 97 follow cases across all types, 41 arise from over_promised , where the documentation promises a capability the implementation never provides. Conversely, semantic_conflict recovers in 13 of its 18 cases. A contradiction in meaning is noticed and worked around far more often than a promised but absent capability. Finding 8. Documentation that promises a capability the implementation never provides accounts for the largest share of follow cases, while semantic conflicts are recovered most often. The type of inconsistency is thus a strong predictor of whether the agent fails.

sections.heading: 7.1. Agent Skills and Skill Ecosystems
sections.text: Agent skills consist of instructions, scripts, and resources that agents dynamically load at inference time to improve task performance ( Anthropic, 2025b ; Anthropic, 2026 ) . Recent research on agent skills generally covers benchmarking, authoring, quality assurance, and security ( Destefanis et al., 2026 ) . Skill benchmark research constructs task collections and interactive environments to evaluate task completion, assessing factors such as absolute pass-rate gains and degradation risks from inference-time skill injection ( Li et al., 2026a ; Han et al., 2026 ; Tank and Nama, 2026 ) . Concurrently, work on skill authoring investigates how to define, reuse, and compose skills in natural language or code, while exploring automated generation, tuning, and evolution to lower authoring costs ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Ding et al., 2026 ) . From a quality perspective, studies treat skill definitions such as SKILL.md as executable artifacts to identify defects (found in 91.8% of 138,133 evaluated skills) ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) by combining static rules, semantic reasoning, and automated repair ( Meng et al., 2026 ) . Finally, security-focused research addresses harmful skills that systematically lower safety refusal rates ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026b ) . in this domain, static detection struggles against adversarial evasion, and although sandboxed dynamic analysis remains the most reliable option ( Ji et al., 2026 ) , existing detection tools still lag behind the rapid pace of threat evolution ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026b ) . Despite these advances across different facets of the agent skill ecosystem, it remains unclear how static inconsistencies in skill definitions surface during runtime. Specifically, existing research lacks a systematic analysis of how agents respond to these defects and how such responses translate into measurable runtime costs ( Dong et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 7.2. Documentation–Code / API Contract Consistency
sections.text: Traditional software engineering research demonstrates that documentation–code inconsistency is pervasive in open-source projects, leading to developer misuse, increased debugging effort, and software defects ( Tan et al., 2007 ; Wen et al., 2019 ) . Existing detection approaches span natural language–code consistency checking ( Tan et al., 2007 ) , LLM-based reverse test generation ( Kiecker et al., 2026 ) , and Ethereum API specification–implementation verification ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . However, as AI agents increasingly serve as direct consumers of tools and APIs, the nature of this problem shifts. Agents rely heavily on textual contracts, modifying a tool’s description alone can alter an agent’s tool selection ( Faghih et al., 2025 ; Sigdel and Baral, 2026 ) . Audits of production APIs reveal that many behavioral constraints exist solely in unstructured prose rather than formal schemas, leading to silent failures that full-loop agents often fail to detect or resolve, ultimately yielding false-negative outputs ( Li et al., 2026c ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . At the same time, agents do not passively succumb to these errors. Enhanced grounding, active verification, and structural guardrails can facilitate recovery, though performance ultimately depends on model capacity, environmental feedback, and task structure ( Naik et al., 2026 ; Tank and Nama, 2026 ) . In dynamic environments with interdependent or unreliable tools, benchmarks indicate that agents frequently suffer from retrieval saturation, overconfidence, skipped validation steps, and failure rationalization ( Li et al., 2026b ) . Consequently, research must explicitly account for agent behavior, recovery, and bypass strategies, re-evaluating how inconsistent specifications impact agent reasoning, execution, and overall system reliability.

sections.heading: 7.3. Agent Reliability and Tool Use
sections.text: Existing research on agent reliability is largely agent-centric. Prior work attributes reliability to reasoning and planning ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , tool selection and invocation ( Qin et al., 2024 ; Patil et al., 2024 ) , benchmarks ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) , and post-failure recovery ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) . Consequently, researchers pursue robustness through better models, prompts, training, or pipelines. Evaluation surveys separate reliability and safety ( Mohammadi et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2026 ) while focusing on dynamic behavior. Meanwhile, failure-mode studies ( Roig, 2025 ) identify archetypes and attribute them to model behavior. A growing body of work connects static artifacts to reliability. Schema-izing prose constraints reduces silent failures ( Li et al., 2026c ) , and agents show high sensitivity to textual tool contracts ( Faghih et al., 2025 ) . Recent years also witness the emergence of static skill auditing ( Wen et al., 2026 ) , skill-behavior attribution ( Tank and Nama, 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) , and interface alignment ( Ren et al., 2026 ) . However, static auditing only targets constraint compliance, and interface alignment addresses runtime presentation. Existing work consequently fails to explain how static quality attributes are exposed upon invocation or how they influence failure, recovery, and bypass. This paper positions itself at the intersection of skill artifact quality and agent behavior. We conduct a white-box static census at the interface layer and treat static artifact quality as an independently auditable variable alongside agent capability to explain agent reliability.

sections.heading: 8.1. Takeaways
sections.text: For Skill Authors. Our results show that the number of inconsistencies does not directly indicate runtime risk. Although roughly two thirds of Skills contain at least one inconsistency, substantial harm is concentrated in a small set of inconsistency types. In particular, over_promised inconsistencies are more likely to be adopted by agents and propagate into failures. When comprehensive auditing is infeasible, authors should therefore prioritize the Document Code boundary, especially cases where documentation promises behavior not supported by the implementation. For conflicts within documentation, authors should identify and unify the authoritative description. For conflicts between documentation and implementation, they should first determine the intended contract and then align the relevant artifacts with it. For Skill Users. The impact of Skill inconsistencies depends on the capability of the model using the Skill. Weaker models are more likely to continue along an incorrect path, so when using Skills that have not been thoroughly validated, users should prefer stronger models or Skills that have already been checked and repaired. Stronger models recover more often, but recovery still incurs additional execution cost. Therefore, in correctness-sensitive or latency-sensitive settings, users should prefer consistent and validated Skills even when using stronger models. For Future Skill Quality Tools. Reporting only the number of inconsistencies provides limited support for risk prioritization. Our results show that runtime risk also depends on inconsistency type, whether the relevant execution path is adopted, and the response capability of the target model. Future tools should therefore combine static findings with execution evidence and stratify findings by runtime risk rather than treating all inconsistencies equally. Beyond reporting how many issues are found, a more useful tool should identify which inconsistencies are more likely to enter execution and lead to follow, recover, or bypass behaviors.

sections.heading: 8.2. Threats to Validity
sections.text: Task construction may increase inconsistency exposure. Our 49 runtime tasks were intentionally designed to trigger the target inconsistency and to reduce the chance that an agent bypasses the relevant path. This design helps measure the effect of an inconsistency once it enters execution, but it does not represent the natural exposure probability in real-world workloads. The high exposure rate observed in RQ3 should therefore be interpreted as a property of controlled defect-exposing tasks rather than as a general exposure rate in practical Skill use. Minimal fixes may still introduce side effects. RQ2 assumes that the main difference between OriginalSkill and FixedSkill is the targeted inconsistency. We reduce this risk through minimal edits and by preventing solution leakage and verifier mirroring. However, even a localized change may improve clarity or alter how an agent interprets the execution path. The difference between FixedSkill and OriginalSkill therefore primarily reflects the targeted inconsistency, but incidental effects of the repair cannot be fully excluded. Trajectory labels are operational approximations of agent behavior. The Exposed, Bypass, Follow, Recover, and BothFail labels in RQ3 are defined from observable execution traces, including file access, changed-file execution, artifact contents, and verifier outcomes. These labels capture external behavior rather than the agent’s internal reasoning. For example, reading a file does not necessarily mean that the agent adopted its contents. Although paired attribution reduces confounding from model-specific behavior, these categories remain operational representations of the underlying runtime mechanisms. The runtime study covers only inconsistencies that can be operationalized as verifiable tasks. RQ1 identifies substantially more inconsistencies than the 49 cases studied in RQ2 and RQ3. Runtime experiments more readily include inconsistencies that can be triggered clearly, repaired minimally, and evaluated with deterministic verifiers. More ambiguous, environment-dependent, or difficult-to-verify inconsistencies may therefore be underrepresented. The runtime results should not be generalized directly to all inconsistency types identified in RQ1.

sections.heading: 9. Conclusion
sections.text: We study contract inconsistencies in Agent Skills through 575 Skills, 1,182 confirmed findings, and 49 runtime tasks across three models. Inconsistencies are widespread, but their runtime impact varies substantially across models. Although agents encounter the Skill in 97.1% of executions, the key difference is post-exposure behavior: models that follow inconsistent content into failure benefit more from fixes, while models that recover are less affected. Static inconsistency counts are thus poor proxies for runtime risk and motivate runtime-aware Skill quality assessment.

LLM agent frameworks heavily rely on external skill assets to standardize tool usage, encode operational workflows, and supply executable runtime resources. Despite their widespread adoption, multi-component skill packages frequently suffer from cross-artifact inconsistencies, where documentation, scripts, and configuration files specify conflicting behavioral constraints. Although static auditing techniques can uncover such contractual discrepancies, static defect volume cannot reliably reflect real-world agent performance degradation. This gap leaves practitioners without rigorous evidence to assess the practical risk of flawed agent skills. This paper presents a systematic empirical study to demystify the runtime implications of skill inconsistencies. We conduct large-scale auditing over 575 community and benchmark skills, yielding 1,182 manually validated contract inconsistencies. We further build a controlled evaluation pipeline with 49 executable agent tasks and three representative LLMs across NoSkill, OriginalSkill, and FixedSkill experimental settings. Through fine-grained behavioral analysis of 441 paired execution trajectories, we quantify the actual performance impacts of resolved defects. Our empirical results reveal that contractual conflicts are pervasive in practical skill ecosystems, impacting over 64% of all examined skills. Skill repairing consistently improves task success rates, yet the performance benefits exhibit strong model heterogeneity, ranging from substantial improvement to negligible gain. Further trajectory dissection indicates that nearly all execution instances expose inconsistent skill content, which rules out exposure frequency as the source of performance variance. Instead, cross-model behavioral differences after inconsistency exposure dominate final task outcomes. We find that weaker models frequently follow erroneous skill specifications and propagate defects into final results, while stronger models actively mitigate runtime errors. Our findings demonstrate that the practical risk of flawed skills is jointly determined by execution reachability and agent post-execution behavior, rather than static inconsistency quantity alone. 1. Introduction Why Agent Skills Matter. LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable components to acquire procedural knowledge, tool-use capabilities, and domain-specific workflows. Agent Skills are an important artifact in this emerging ecosystem ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2026a ) . Unlike one-off prompts, a Skill is typically distributed as a reusable package containing documentation, metadata, scripts, configuration files, and other resources ( Anthropic, 2026 ; Anthropic, 2025b ) . Together, these artifacts specify how the Skill should be discovered, interpreted, and executed. As the public Skill ecosystem rapidly expands, the same Skill may be reused across different tasks and agents, allowing quality issues to affect multiple downstream executions. This multi-artifact structure also introduces a new reliability challenge. Because individual artifacts can evolve independently, they may make incompatible claims about the same functionality, interface, or runtime requirement. For example, documentation may promise a capability that the implementation does not provide, or different documents may specify conflicting dependency versions. We refer to such cases as Skill contract inconsistencies . Unlike conventional specification-implementation mismatches, these inconsistencies may arise between a Skill and its environment, across documentation artifacts, or between documentation and code. Do Static Inconsistencies Matter at Runtime? Detecting a static inconsistency does not imply that it will cause runtime harm. Static inspection can establish that two artifacts conflict, but it cannot determine whether the conflict will enter actual execution or whether it will ultimately affect task outcomes or execution cost. A static finding therefore indicates a potential problem, not its actual runtime risk. This distinction has direct practical consequences. If all inconsistencies are treated equally, limited auditing and repair effort cannot be prioritized toward findings that actually affect execution, while low-impact findings may obscure more consequential ones. Skill quality assessment therefore needs to move beyond finding detection toward runtime risk prioritization. Existing work has examined Skill structure ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , documentation quality ( Li et al., 2026a ) , security ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026b ) , and artifact-level defects ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Meng et al., 2026 ) . However, there is still limited evidence on whether such static findings enter agent execution, whether repairing them changes runtime outcomes, and how agents respond after exposure. We therefore lack a systematic understanding of how static defects translate into runtime consequences : how prevalent Skill contract inconsistencies are, how much they affect agent execution, and why these effects arise. Our Study and Key Findings. To answer these questions, we conduct an empirical study of Skill contract inconsistencies. First, we collect 575 Skills from GitHub and SkillBench ( Li et al., 2026a ) and develop a taxonomy spanning three contract boundaries: Environment, Inter Document, and Document Code. Through automated auditing and manual validation, we confirm 1,182 inconsistencies and characterize their prevalence, types, and distribution. Second, we construct 49 verifiable tasks from real-world Skills and evaluate three models under three conditions: NoSkill , OriginalSkill , and FixedSkill . The comparison between OriginalSkill and FixedSkill estimates the runtime effect of the targeted inconsistency, while NoSkill separates this effect from the general benefit of using a Skill. Finally, we analyze paired execution trajectories to trace whether inconsistencies enter execution and how different responses relate to final outcomes. Our study yields four main findings. ❶ Skill contract inconsistencies are widespread and unevenly distributed. At least one inconsistency appears in 67.4% of GitHub Skills and 64.4% of SkillBench Skills. In SkillBench, Document Code inconsistencies account for 56.2% of all findings, with over_promised alone accounting for 45.6%. ❷ Fixing inconsistencies improves average task effectiveness for all three models, but the magnitude varies substantially. Claude Haiku 4.5 ( Anthropic, 2025a ) , Qwen3.6-35B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ; oMLX, 2026 ) , and DeepSeek-V4-Flash ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026 ; Continuum Labs, 2026 ; Hanks, 2026 ) improve by 0.136, 0.085, and 0.023 score points, respectively. The runtime impact of an inconsistency is therefore not a fixed property of the Skill alone. ❸ These cross-model differences are not explained by Skill exposure. Across 441 paired executions, agents read the Skill in 97.1% of runs. Exposure rates are similarly high for Haiku, Qwen, and DeepSeek at 98%, 93%, and 100%, respectively. ❹ The models diverge primarily after contact. Haiku, Qwen, and DeepSeek follow the inconsistency into failure in 30%, 24%, and 12% of runs, respectively, while DeepSeek recovers in 56% of exposed runs. The key distinction is therefore not whether an agent encounters the inconsistency, but how it responds after exposure. Taken together, these findings show that static inconsistency count is a poor proxy for runtime risk. Runtime impact depends not only on whether an inconsistency exists, but also on whether it enters execution and how the agent responds after contact. Skill quality assessment should therefore move beyond counting static findings toward distinguishing their actual runtime risks. Contributions. In summary, this work makes the following contributions: ∙ \bullet A taxonomy and large-scale empirical characterization of Skill contract inconsistencies. We develop a taxonomy spanning three artifact boundaries and systematically analyze 1,182 manually confirmed inconsistencies across 575 real-world and benchmark Skills. ∙ \bullet A controlled evaluation of the runtime impact of Skill inconsistencies. We construct 49 real-world tasks and quantify the effects of inconsistencies on task effectiveness and execution efficiency across three models under NoSkill , OriginalSkill , and FixedSkill conditions. ∙ \bullet An execution-level account of how static inconsistencies translate into runtime impact. Through trajectory analysis, we trace inconsistencies from exposure to outcome and show that cross-model differences arise from post-exposure behavior rather than Skill exposure itself. 2. Background and Motivation 2.1. Agent Skills Agent Skills are reusable execution units that provide LLM agents with structured procedural knowledge, tool usage logic, and domain-specific task workflows. Unlike ordinary prompts that provide guidance for a single request, a Skill packages multiple interdependent artifacts into a self-contained unit that an agent can discover, load, and execute. A typical Skill is organized as a directory centered on a SKILL.md file. Its YAML frontmatter specifies metadata such as the Skill name, functionality, applicable scenarios, and dependencies, while the body describes execution steps, constraints, and expected outcomes. A Skill may also include scripts, configuration files, static resources, and other supporting artifacts. Figure 1 . The workflow of using Skills. As shown in Figure 1 , an agent first identifies candidate Skills for a given task and determines their applicability from the associated metadata. It then reads the relevant instructions and resources, executes the prescribed workflow or code, and completes the task according to the requirements stated by the Skill. A Skill is therefore more than a single textual prompt. Its documentation, code, resources, and environment requirements collectively define its expected behavior, while these artifacts may evolve independently. Reliable Skill execution depends not only on the correctness of each artifact, but also on whether they remain consistent about the same behavioral requirements. 2.2. A Motivating Example From the perspective of an executing agent, the documentation, metadata, code, and resources packaged within a Skill collectively form an implicit Skill contract . This contract specifies the behavioral commitments made by the Skill, including its functionality, inputs and outputs, execution procedure, dependencies, and runtime requirements. A Skill contract combines natural language, semi-structured configuration, and executable code. We define a contract inconsistency as a case in which two or more artifacts make incompatible claims about the same contract property. Such inconsistencies may arise between environment requirements and actual dependencies, across documentation artifacts, or between documentation and code. However, the static presence of an inconsistency does not imply runtime failure. File inspection can establish that conflicting claims exist, but it cannot determine whether the inconsistency will enter the agent’s execution path or what effect it will eventually have. Figure 2 . A real-world Skill. ① marks an Inter Document inconsistency, while ② and ③ mark Document Code inconsistencies. To illustrate this problem, we use the real-world d3-visualization Skill. Figure 2 shows three inconsistencies that can be identified through static inspection. ❶ Document-internal version conflict. One part of the documentation states that the Skill uses D3.js v6, while another specifies d3@7.9.0 as the default dependency. These statements make incompatible claims about the same dependency version and therefore form an Inter Document inconsistency. ❷ Document Code inconsistency in sorting behavior. The documentation requires deterministic sorting before binding input rows to visual elements. However, bubble_chart_example.js directly constructs a Set from the input values without performing the required sorting. The resulting element order may therefore depend on the input order. ❸ Document Code inconsistency in force layout determinism. The documentation requires a fixed number of iterations, deterministic initial positions, and termination after the specified number of iterations. The corresponding code neither fixes the initial randomness nor enforces the specified iteration count. It therefore cannot guarantee the deterministic behavior described by the documentation. This example leads to three observations. Observation 1. Skill contract inconsistencies are not limited to documentation and code. The first inconsistency exists entirely within the documentation and does not involve implementation behavior. This shows that Skill inconsistencies extend beyond conventional specification implementation mismatches. Understanding consistency problems in Skills therefore requires examining conflicts across multiple artifact boundaries. Observation 2. Static detectability does not reveal runtime impact. All three inconsistencies can be detected before execution, yet static evidence cannot determine whether they affect agent execution. It remains unclear whether such inconsistencies reduce task effectiveness, increase execution cost, or affect agents with different capabilities differently. Detecting an inconsistency therefore establishes only that a potential problem exists, not how much it matters at runtime. Observation 3. Final outcomes do not explain how runtime impact arises. Even when an inconsistency is associated with a change in task outcome, success or failure does not explain how that effect arises. We do not know whether the inconsistency enters the agent’s execution path or how the agent responds after encountering the content. Understanding this process requires tracing how the inconsistency propagates through execution and how the agent responds to it. Together, these observations reveal three open questions. We need to understand what inconsistencies exist in real Skills, how much they affect agent execution, and how those effects arise. We therefore ask the following Research Questions (RQs): ∙ \bullet RQ1 (Prevalence and Characteristics). How prevalent are contract inconsistencies in Agent Skills, and what forms do they take? ∙ \bullet RQ2 (Runtime Impact). To what extent do Skill contract inconsistencies affect the task effectiveness and execution efficiency of agents with different capabilities? ∙ \bullet RQ3 (Impact Mechanisms). When and why do Skill contract inconsistencies affect agent execution? 3. Study Methodology Figure 3 provides an end-to-end overview of our study pipeline. We first build a Skill dataset from GitHub and SkillBench and identify contract inconsistencies through taxonomy-guided SkillAudit and manual validation. RQ1 characterizes the prevalence, types, and distribution of these confirmed findings. We then transform selected real-world inconsistencies into triggerable and verifiable runtime tasks and construct minimally repaired counterparts. RQ2 evaluates their effects on task effectiveness and execution efficiency under NoSkill , OriginalSkill , and FixedSkill conditions. Finally, RQ3 analyzes paired execution trajectories to determine how inconsistencies enter execution and how agents respond after exposure. Figure 3 . The Study pipeline of the paper. 3.1. Data Collection We construct our dataset from GitHub and SkillBench to cover both naturally evolved real-world Skills and manually designed benchmark Skills. The final dataset contains 575 Skills. GitHub Skill Collection. We sample community-maintained Skills from open-source GitHub repositories, prioritizing repositories with high star counts as a proxy for community visibility and practical use. To capture structural differences, we divide candidate Skills into two groups. Document-only Skills contain only Markdown documentation, without executable scripts or supplementary resources. Resource-augmented Skills additionally include internal artifacts such as scripts, configuration files, or other supporting resources. To reduce repository-level bias, we sample at most three Skills from each repository. We inspect Skill metadata and functional descriptions during selection and avoid choosing highly overlapping Skills from the same repository. This process yields 488 GitHub Skills. 3.1.2. SkillBench Collection. We further include 87 Skills from SkillBench ( Li et al., 2026a ) . Unlike community Skills that evolve naturally on GitHub, SkillBench Skills are manually authored and paired with explicit task objectives and ground-truth specifications, providing a more controlled Skill corpus. This difference provides a useful contrast for RQ1. The GitHub corpus reflects consistency problems that arise during real-world development and maintenance, whereas SkillBench is manually constructed and reviewed, and therefore represents a more controlled artifact-quality setting. Comparing the two allows us to examine whether contract inconsistencies are primarily artifacts of real-world maintenance noise or remain common even in curated Skills. 3.1.3. Data Summary. Across both sources, we obtain 575 Skills, as shown in Table 1 . Following the taxonomy used by SkillBench ( Li et al., 2026a ) , we categorize them into eight domains: Software Engineering, Media & Content Production, Finance & Economics, Cybersecurity, Office & White Collar Work, Industrial & Physical Systems, Natural Science, and Mathematics & Operations Research. 3.2. Skill Contract Inconsistency Identification RQ1 first requires a consistent definition of Skill contract inconsistency and a reliable way to identify such cases at scale. We therefore construct an inconsistency taxonomy, operationalize it through a taxonomy-guided static audit pipeline, and manually validate the resulting findings. Figure 4 . Taxonomy of skill - level inconsistencies. 3.2.1. Taxonomy Of Skill Inconsistency We construct the taxonomy through iterative qualitative analysis ( Raj et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . Starting from real-world Skill artifacts, including documentation, configuration, and source code, we manually inspect misalignment patterns and synthesize them with known issue patterns from tool-agent and API-contract literature ( Kiecker et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . During iteration, we merge redundant categories, eliminate overlapping definitions, and refine the decision criteria for each class. We first classify inconsistencies by the participants of the violated contract: ∙ \bullet Environmental layer: Skill vs. runtime environment. ∙ \bullet Inter-document layer: conflicts among descriptive documents. ∙ \bullet Document-code layer: documentation vs. implementation. Within the Document-code layer, we further classify inconsistencies by the direction of deviation: ∙ \bullet Over-promised (Doc > > Code). The documentation promises functionality, constraints, or behavior that the implementation does not provide. ∙ \bullet Semantically-conflicting (Doc ≠ \neq Code). The documentation and implementation both specify the relevant behavior but contradict each other semantically. ∙ \bullet Under-promised (Doc < < Code). The implementation provides capabilities that are not documented. Because this study focuses on contract violations that may affect agent execution, we primarily retain over-promised and semantically-conflicting cases. Under-promised cases are typically benign ( He et al., 2026 ) and are suppressed by default. We also exclude failures caused purely by agent hallucination or external-service faults ( Tian and Chen, 2026 ) , as these do not originate from inconsistency among Skill artifacts. The resulting taxonomy is shown in Figure 4 . 3.2.2. Audit Tool To audit skill consistency, we design an tool named SkillAudit. SkillAudit operationalizes the proposed inconsistency taxonomy in 3.2.1 . It takes a skill package as input and outputs ranked findings mapped directly to canonical taxonomy classes. The tool performs purely static analysis without executing the target skill or requiring ground truth. Its pipeline comprises four sequential modules sharing a unified intermediate representation: ❶ Package Comprehension. This module parses documentation and source code into a structured SkillMap. A scanner first validates the target directory (requiring at least one ‘SKILL.md‘), filters out metadata, caches and binaries, and retains partial file contents for indexing. A two-round LLM agent then builds the SkillMap of components, sub-skills and relations: round one selects files for full reading; round two generates the structured map. The SkillMap is cached via content hashing to eliminate redundant model calls for unchanged packages. ❷ Inconsistency Detection. Two groups of checkers identify taxonomy-defined inconsistencies over the same evidence base. Four deterministic checkers perform AST-based code analysis, schema comparison, environment constraint checking, and execution-path URL validation. Five independent LLM checkers target different taxonomy categories and inspect semantic conflicts across artifacts. All detections are normalized to canonical taxonomy labels, while duplicate evidence from different checkers is retained for later aggregation. ❸ Adjudication and Aggregation. This module refines raw detections into structured findings. An adjudicator reviews LLM findings in batches, assigning confirmed or suppressed verdicts with adjusted severity and evidence strength. Rule-based suppression is tracked separately. The adjudicator uses a fail-open design: errors preserve original findings to avoid silent defect loss. Aggregation follows two stages: exact-key deduplication, then semantic clustering by class, location and evidence overlap. Each cluster forms a single root cause entry listing all contributing checkers. ❹ Reporting. The final reporting module produces reports with inconsistencies, root cause statistics, evidence strength distribution, and token usage. Each finding includes a taxonomy label, line-numbered evidence, rationale and evidence strength. Evidence strength is structurally enforced: only verified findings may claim execution blocking. Deterministic checkers run standalone without credentials or network access, ensuring full reproducibility. 3.2.3. Manual Validation To verify the final auditting results, two authors independently reviewed the audit reports of skills drawn from the full pipeline output of audit tool. with a third resolving disagreements. Of the 575 skills in the datasets, 1182 inconsistencies were confirmed finally. 3.3. Task Construction WildSkills contains 49 dynamically verifiable task instances, all derived from GitHub Skills. Each task materializes a single re-verified inconsistency so that the experiment focuses on the effect of that inconsistency rather than the overall quality of the Skill. Each task is constructed in five stages. ❶ Selection. Candidate inconsistencies are drawn from manually confirmed GitHub findings. Before inclusion, we re-check the current Skill files to ensure that the target inconsistency still exists and can be localized precisely. ❷ Trigger Design. We write a realistic user request whose most direct solution requires the artifact or code path associated with the target inconsistency. We also size the input so that bypassing the Skill and manually recomputing the result is more expensive than using the Skill, reducing opportunities to sidestep the defect. ❸ Environment. The shipped Skill, project workspace, and input data are packaged into a Docker environment. The Skill is mounted at runtime rather than baked into the image, allowing all experimental conditions to share the same environment while differing only in the provided Skill. ❹ Verifier. Each task includes a deterministic verifier that checks the produced artifact against the target contract using programmatic assertions only. No LLM-as-a-judge is used. ❺ Oracle. We construct a reference solution that passes all verifier checks, confirming that the task itself is solvable and that failure does not arise from an infeasible specification. This process converts a static finding into a repeatable runtime question: what happens when the target inconsistency is placed on a relevant execution path? 3.3.1. Counterfactual Skill Repair To estimate the runtime impact of each target inconsistency, we construct a minimally repaired FixedSkill for every OriginalSkill . The goal is not to redesign the Skill, but to remove the target inconsistency while changing as little else as possible. The repair strategy depends on the violated contract boundary. For an environmental inconsistency , we align the Skill with the actual runtime environment and pin the relevant requirement. For an inter-document inconsistency , we identify an authoritative statement and unify conflicting descriptions while leaving the implementation unchanged. For a document-code inconsistency , we first determine the intended contract and then modify the implementation to satisfy it. When the documented promise cannot be supported under the target environment, we instead narrow the documentation to match the feasible behavior. All repairs follow two constraints. First, each edit is minimal and confined to the inconsistent element. Second, the repair must not leak the task solution or mirror the verifier. Each WildSkills task therefore has a semantically matched OriginalSkill and FixedSkill , forming the basis for controlled comparison. 3.4. Models and Experimental Conditions We evaluate three models: DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Their performance on benchmarks and on our NoSkill baseline allows us to examine whether inconsistency impact varies across models, as shown in Table 2 . We emphasize within-model comparisons. The Qwen deployment uses 4-bit quantization, while DeepSeek-V4-Flash runs in its default non-thinking configuration. Absolute cross-model differences should therefore be interpreted with caution. Each task is packaged as a fixed experimental unit containing the user instruction, workspace, Skill directory, deterministic verifier, and oracle solution, and is executed in an isolated Docker container. The agent runs as an unprivileged user, and the Skill directory is injected only at runtime. Table 2 . Models and baseline performance. The repaired Skill with the target inconsistency removed is provided. The paired comparison between OriginalSkill and FixedSkill estimates the runtime effect of the target inconsistency, while NoSkill measures the effect of using the Skill relative to having no Skill. All runs use the same execution harness and a uniform budget covering generation requests, cumulative tokens, and output tokens. Each task-condition combination is executed with three replicates to reduce stochastic variation. 3.5. Metrics Effectiveness. Our primary metric is verifier pass rate, defined as the fraction of deterministic checks satisfied by the produced artifact, ranging from 0 to 1. For each task-condition pair, we first average the three technical replicates and then perform task-level paired comparisons. The fix effect is defined as Δ = Fixed − Original \Delta=\textsc{Fixed}-\textsc{Original} . This yields 49 paired task-level observations per model. Efficiency. We record cumulative input and output tokens, API calls, agent turns, and wall-clock time. Runs that reach the per-run budget limit are treated as truncated and reported separately. For non-truncated runs, we report median execution costs and additionally use tokens per score point to capture the relationship between computational cost and task effectiveness. 3.6. For each task, the fix diff yields three signal types: the files the fix changed, code-like tokens present only in the shipped skill ( shipped-only anchors ), and tokens present only in the fixed skill ( fixed-only anchors ), together with the verifier checks tied to the changed behaviour. Second, response is attributed by pairing : a behaviour is attributed to the inconsistency only when the FixedSkill arm of the same cell does not exhibit it, which separates the inconsistency’s contribution from a model’s unconditional habits.
