Agent Skills and Skill Ecosystems Agent skills consist of instructions, scripts, and resources that agents dynamically load at inference time to improve task performance ( Anthropic, 2025b ; Anthropic, 2026 ) . Recent research on agent skills generally covers benchmarking, authoring, quality assurance, and security ( Destefanis et al., 2026 ) . Skill benchmark research constructs task collections and interactive environments to evaluate task completion, assessing factors such as absolute pass-rate gains and degradation risks from inference-time skill injection ( Li et al., 2026a ; Han et al., 2026 ; Tank and Nama, 2026 ) . Concurrently, work on skill authoring investigates how to define, reuse, and compose skills in natural language or code, while exploring automated generation, tuning, and evolution to lower authoring costs ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Ding et al., 2026 ) . From a quality perspective, studies treat skill definitions such as SKILL.md as executable artifacts to identify defects (found in 91.8% of 138,133 evaluated skills) ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) by combining static rules, semantic reasoning, and automated repair ( Meng et al., 2026 ) . Finally, security-focused research addresses harmful skills that systematically lower safety refusal rates ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026b ) . in this domain, static detection struggles against adversarial evasion, and although sandboxed dynamic analysis remains the most reliable option ( Ji et al., 2026 ) , existing detection tools still lag behind the rapid pace of threat evolution ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026b ) . Despite these advances across different facets of the agent skill ecosystem, it remains unclear how static inconsistencies in skill definitions surface during runtime. Specifically, existing research lacks a systematic analysis of how agents respond to these defects and how such responses translate into measurable runtime costs ( Dong et al., 2026 ) . 7.2. Documentation–Code / API Contract Consistency Traditional software engineering research demonstrates that documentation–code inconsistency is pervasive in open-source projects, leading to developer misuse, increased debugging effort, and software defects ( Tan et al., 2007 ; Wen et al., 2019 ) . Existing detection approaches span natural language–code consistency checking ( Tan et al., 2007 ) , LLM-based reverse test generation ( Kiecker et al., 2026 ) , and Ethereum API specification–implementation verification ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . However, as AI agents increasingly serve as direct consumers of tools and APIs, the nature of this problem shifts. Agents rely heavily on textual contracts, modifying a tool’s description alone can alter an agent’s tool selection ( Faghih et al., 2025 ; Sigdel and Baral, 2026 ) . Audits of production APIs reveal that many behavioral constraints exist solely in unstructured prose rather than formal schemas, leading to silent failures that full-loop agents often fail to detect or resolve, ultimately yielding false-negative outputs ( Li et al., 2026c ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . At the same time, agents do not passively succumb to these errors. Enhanced grounding, active verification, and structural guardrails can facilitate recovery, though performance ultimately depends on model capacity, environmental feedback, and task structure ( Naik et al., 2026 ; Tank and Nama, 2026 ) . In dynamic environments with interdependent or unreliable tools, benchmarks indicate that agents frequently suffer from retrieval saturation, overconfidence, skipped validation steps, and failure rationalization ( Li et al., 2026b ) . Consequently, research must explicitly account for agent behavior, recovery, and bypass strategies, re-evaluating how inconsistent specifications impact agent reasoning, execution, and overall system reliability. 7.3. Agent Reliability and Tool Use Existing research on agent reliability is largely agent-centric. Prior work attributes reliability to reasoning and planning ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , tool selection and invocation ( Qin et al., 2024 ; Patil et al., 2024 ) , benchmarks ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) , and post-failure recovery ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) . Consequently, researchers pursue robustness through better models, prompts, training, or pipelines. Evaluation surveys separate reliability and safety ( Mohammadi et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2026 ) while focusing on dynamic behavior. Meanwhile, failure-mode studies ( Roig, 2025 ) identify archetypes and attribute them to model behavior. A growing body of work connects static artifacts to reliability. Schema-izing prose constraints reduces silent failures ( Li et al., 2026c ) , and agents show high sensitivity to textual tool contracts ( Faghih et al., 2025 ) . Recent years also witness the emergence of static skill auditing ( Wen et al., 2026 ) , skill-behavior attribution ( Tank and Nama, 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) , and interface alignment ( Ren et al., 2026 ) . However, static auditing only targets constraint compliance, and interface alignment addresses runtime presentation. Existing work consequently fails to explain how static quality attributes are exposed upon invocation or how they influence failure, recovery, and bypass. This paper positions itself at the intersection of skill artifact quality and agent behavior. We conduct a white-box static census at the interface layer and treat static artifact quality as an independently auditable variable alongside agent capability to explain agent reliability. 8. Discussion 8.1. Takeaways For Skill Authors. Our results show that the number of inconsistencies does not directly indicate runtime risk. Although roughly two thirds of Skills contain at least one inconsistency, substantial harm is concentrated in a small set of inconsistency types. In particular, over_promised inconsistencies are more likely to be adopted by agents and propagate into failures. When comprehensive auditing is infeasible, authors should therefore prioritize the Document Code boundary, especially cases where documentation promises behavior not supported by the implementation. For conflicts within documentation, authors should identify and unify the authoritative description. For conflicts between documentation and implementation, they should first determine the intended contract and then align the relevant artifacts with it. For Skill Users. The impact of Skill inconsistencies depends on the capability of the model using the Skill. Weaker models are more likely to continue along an incorrect path, so when using Skills that have not been thoroughly validated, users should prefer stronger models or Skills that have already been checked and repaired. Stronger models recover more often, but recovery still incurs additional execution cost. Therefore, in correctness-sensitive or latency-sensitive settings, users should prefer consistent and validated Skills even when using stronger models. For Future Skill Quality Tools. Reporting only the number of inconsistencies provides limited support for risk prioritization. Our results show that runtime risk also depends on inconsistency type, whether the relevant execution path is adopted, and the response capability of the target model. Future tools should therefore combine static findings with execution evidence and stratify findings by runtime risk rather than treating all inconsistencies equally. Beyond reporting how many issues are found, a more useful tool should identify which inconsistencies are more likely to enter execution and lead to follow, recover, or bypass behaviors. 8.2. Threats to Validity Task construction may increase inconsistency exposure. Our 49 runtime tasks were intentionally designed to trigger the target inconsistency and to reduce the chance that an agent bypasses the relevant path. This design helps measure the effect of an inconsistency once it enters execution, but it does not represent the natural exposure probability in real-world workloads. The high exposure rate observed in RQ3 should therefore be interpreted as a property of controlled defect-exposing tasks rather than as a general exposure rate in practical Skill use. Minimal fixes may still introduce side effects. RQ2 assumes that the main difference between OriginalSkill and FixedSkill is the targeted inconsistency. We reduce this risk through minimal edits and by preventing solution leakage and verifier mirroring. However, even a localized change may improve clarity or alter how an agent interprets the execution path. The difference between FixedSkill and OriginalSkill therefore primarily reflects the targeted inconsistency, but incidental effects of the repair cannot be fully excluded. Trajectory labels are operational approximations of agent behavior. The Exposed, Bypass, Follow, Recover, and BothFail labels in RQ3 are defined from observable execution traces, including file access, changed-file execution, artifact contents, and verifier outcomes. These labels capture external behavior rather than the agent’s internal reasoning. For example, reading a file does not necessarily mean that the agent adopted its contents. Although paired attribution reduces confounding from model-specific behavior, these categories remain operational representations of the underlying runtime mechanisms. The runtime study covers only inconsistencies that can be operationalized as verifiable tasks. RQ1 identifies substantially more inconsistencies than the 49 cases studied in RQ2 and RQ3. Runtime experiments more readily include inconsistencies that can be triggered clearly, repaired minimally, and evaluated with deterministic verifiers. More ambiguous, environment-dependent, or difficult-to-verify inconsistencies may therefore be underrepresented. The runtime results should not be generalized directly to all inconsistency types identified in RQ1. 9. Conclusion We study contract inconsistencies in Agent Skills through 575 Skills, 1,182 confirmed findings, and 49 runtime tasks across three models. Inconsistencies are widespread, but their runtime impact varies substantially across models. Although agents encounter the Skill in 97.1% of executions, the key difference is post-exposure behavior: models that follow inconsistent content into failure benefit more from fixes, while models that recover are less affected. Static inconsistency counts are thus poor proxies for runtime risk and motivate runtime-aware Skill quality assessment.
